searches.note: Thirty three searches of a share of forty five, twelve left unspent, none of them the author's. Seven were restricted to a house's own domain or to HistoryLink (eroicawine.com with ste-michelle.com, drloosen.com and smwe.com once, quilcedacreek.com twice, leonetticellar.com twice, historylink.org once, woodwardcanyon.com with greatnorthwestwine.com and historylink.org once) and are read through their summaries; four kept the house's own domain out (quilcedacreek.com, leonetticellar.com, woodwardcanyon.com, cayusevineyards.com twice in all, and the Eroica houses once) so that the second source would be independent; the rest went to the open web. The one shared search is L'Ecole No 41 of 1983, which the Leonetti and Woodward Canyon records both teach; the Champoux search serves Quilceda Creek and Woodward Canyon and is counted under Quilceda. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

History went first to the open web with the house's own domain kept out, so that each date found a second source beside the house; the making and the sites went to the house's own sheets, read through their search summaries, and to merchants and critics' houses where the sheets were silent.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source (the Grenache rosé of 1967, Cold Creek begun in 1972, Leonetti's first vintage and its oak, Woodward Canyon's share in Champoux); where a detail was found in no source of this check it was cut or said with less (the slow ripening of Eroica's cooler sites, the slow ferment at Cayuse, Mach One's planting, the fruit Quilceda took in 1986, Leonetti's respelling).

Where the check met a fact the author had left out and two sources carried it, it was added only where it teaches a turning point: the Los Angeles Times as the organiser of the tasting of 1974, Leonetti's Cabernet first in a national tasting in December 1982, Woodward Canyon among the owners of Champoux from 1996, Cayuse farming biodynamically from 2002, Serra Pedace first planted in 2010.

The dead are named with dates only where the author had them (André Tchelistcheff, Beethoven); every living person stays described. Sources whose title or address names a living person, a writer's own site and every review with a score were met among the results and are cited neither in the fragment nor here; HistoryLink's interviews are cited under the winery's name, never the person's.

tested: The two Seattle firms of 1934 and their merger of 1954 as American Wine Growers: the Wine Commission's timeline gives 1954 for the merger, HistoryLink and the Northwest Wine Report give 1940 for the merger and the new name some fifteen years later, and HistoryLink gives 1933 to 1935 for the firms. Changed: the name is dated to the mid 1950s; 1934 stays as the company's account.

The launch of 1967, its four wines and Tchelistcheff as consultant: the Wine Commission (a new line of premium vinifera wines called Ste. Michelle Vintners), Great Northwest Wine and the company's history (Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Semillon and a Grenache rosé), and several accounts that he consulted from 1967. Changed: Grenache becomes Grenache rosé.

Cold Creek planted in 1973: the company's history page begins the planting in 1972, its press release of 2013 dates the original planting to 1973, and a third account gives 1972 through 1973; the doubling of the state's plantings is in the company's release and Great Northwest Wine. Changed to began planting in 1972; the hedge on the doubling stays.
The 1974 tasting won by the 1972 Riesling: the house's Riesling page and Great Northwest Wine name a blind tasting held by the Los Angeles Times. Confirmed and the organiser added.

The move of 1976 to Woodinville and the lumber baron's estate of 1912: HistoryLink, the company's timeline and the National Register's date for the manor house. Confirmed; the baron stays unnamed, as the author had him.

Eroica from the 1999 vintage with Dr. Loosen: Dr. Loosen's own page and The Herald on twenty years of Eroica; the producer printed as Chateau Ste. Michelle and Dr. Loosen on merchants' listings and Decanter's. Confirmed, and the label term stands.

The sites: the Eroica vineyards page says the early blends were mostly Cold Creek, a warm site, and that cooler vineyards are consistent candidates now. Confirmed in part; the growers' slow ripening for flavour was found nowhere and is cut.

The making: steel ageing of some ten months in the 2024 sheet, on lees and partly native yeast in 2025, and one vintage summary with a part in clay amphora and concrete. Changed to chiefly in stainless steel, with no claim of no oak.
Off dry with high acidity: Wine Peeps (residual sugar about 1.6 per cent), Wine Enthusiast (technically off dry, low pH, high acid) and merchants. Confirmed; no figure printed.
Eroica Ice Wine from grapes frozen on the vine and pressed while frozen: the company's release and merchants. Confirmed.
The ageing: a vertical of 2026 found the 1999 still fresh, so ten years or so understated it. Changed to a decade and more.

The questions: the wine question's four reasons for sweetness and freshness, one right, the Ice Wine named as the sweet one; the story question's four Washington towns, Woodinville the key. Sound; the explanation's Cold Creek date follows the story.

The rules: Dr. Loosen is a house name and stands; the living partner and the company's present owners are not named; no score (the Top 100 lists of the first vintages met in search are left out). Sound.

tested: Founded in 1978 at Snohomish, first vintage 1979 made in the family garage: Wikipedia, Wine Spectator and the house's history; one merchant says bonded in 1979, and HistoryLink has the predecessor registered as Cedar Ridge Winery in 1978. Confirmed.

The founder a nephew of Tchelistcheff on his mother's side, the uncle guiding the family: Wikipedia and Wine Spectator for the nephew, a wine wiki and the house for the mother's side, and the wiki adds that Tchelistcheff sponsored the family's move to the United States in 1946. Confirmed.
The twelfth bonded winery in Washington since Prohibition: the house's history and a second account met in the same search. Confirmed as the house's count.

Mercer vineyard of 1972, later Champoux, fruit from 1986: the house's history and HistoryLink's interview (offered a little fruit from the Mercer vineyard in 1986); Wikipedia and Great Northwest Wine give the Mercers' first Cabernet block of 1972. Confirmed; and took all it could cut, since the interview says a little fruit was offered.

The company of 1996: Wikipedia, HistoryLink and Great Northwest Wine on the vineyard give the Champoux family's partnership of 1996 with Andrew Will, Powers, Quilceda Creek and Woodward Canyon, one account 1997. Confirmed; the house's first share of 1997 stays as the house tells it.

Twenty to twenty two months in new French oak: the house's sheets for 2000, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2009, 2010 and 2020 (twenty two months) and 2016 and 2017 (twenty months), all new French oak. Confirmed; the fermentation is in none of them.
Cabernet with a little Merlot in some years: the 2006 sheet (97 and 3) and the 2016 and 2017 (all Cabernet); Champoux the heart of the 2020 with the rest from Mach One. Confirmed.
CVR named from the 2009 vintage, from younger vines and barrels set aside: the house's 2009 and 2004 CVR pages. Confirmed.

Galitzine and Mach One planted in the 2000s, set close: the house's Galitzine page (2001 and 2002, one sheet 2000 and 2001, close spacing, first bottled alone with the 2004 vintage). Galitzine confirmed and dated; Mach One's planting found nowhere and cut from the story.

The questions: four places for the fruit, Champoux the key and Snohomish the trap; four Napa winemakers of Tchelistcheff's years for the uncle, the explanation naming Joe Heitz as his assistant at Beaulieu. Sound.

The rules: the founder, his wife and his son stay described; the table's It shows what pure Washington Cabernet can be is a judgement and is cut; the perfect scores of the library's line stay out; the house's own news of full ownership of Champoux in 2026 is volatile and stays out. Sound after the change.
